problem: The rule states flatly that a three-byte instruction takes 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 T. That holds for JMP/LXI but not for the common three-byte instructions that also touch memory or the stack. LDA 2050H and STA 2050H need a fourth machine cycle (memory read or memory write), so they take 13 T, and CALL 2000H pushes the return address, so it takes 18 T. The chapter lists only two corrections, so a student will answer 10 T for LDA and lose marks.
fix: Soften the rule and add a third correction: 'Most one-byte instructions take 4 T, many two-byte instructions 7 T, and many three-byte instructions 10 T. Three corrections keep counts honest. (1) Some one-byte instructions take 6, 10 or 12 T for internal work or stack traffic with no operand fetch. (2) An I/O instruction uses an I/O read or write cycle, still 3 T, with IO/M high. (3) Instructions that move data to or from memory or the stack add further machine cycles: LDA 2050H and STA 2050H are 13 T (OF + MR + MR + MR/MW) and CALL 2000H is 18 T (OF + MR + MR + MW + MW).'

problem: The sentence says all five machine cycles begin with the high address byte on A15-A8 and the low address byte on AD7-AD0. In the two I/O cycles A15-A8 does not carry a high address byte: the same 8-bit port address is placed on both A15-A8 and AD7-AD0, as the I/O bullets later say. A student meets two different statements about the same wires.
fix: In a memory cycle the CPU puts the high address byte on A15-A8 and the low address byte on AD7-AD0, and raises ALE. In an I/O cycle it puts the same 8-bit port address on both A15-A8 and AD7-AD0, and still raises ALE.
